## GHG EMISSIONS ASSESSMENT

The single largest obstacle to realizing our climate goals is that the price of fossil fuels does not reflect the true cost of carbon, which is realized in increasing threats to our health, polluted air and water, and damage to property and infrastructure. These costs are disproportionately borne by communities of color and low-income residents. The City of Seattle does not current have a city-wide policy for tracking the carbon impacts of policies or projects, which limits our ability to fully understand the cost or savings related to carbon emissions.

## Assess GHG Emissions Impact of City decisions

Issue an Executive Order directing City departments to assess the GHG emissions impact of City plans, policies, and major investments.

City policies, plans and major investments have wide reaching and long-term climate impacts.  However, the City lacks a systematic way to assess the GHG emissions associated with major City actions, and to consider the cost of those emissions during the planning process. Creating such a system would help the City make better decisions in the short-term and be prepared for future financial impacts, such as carbon pricing. The Mayor will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with departments to define the types of projects to assess, the assessment method, and how to account for the broader costs of carbon, by October 2018.

## BUILDINGS

Building energy use represents one-third of Seattle's GHG emissions. Since 2005, the city has benefitted from Seattle City Light's carbon neutral electricity. City Light offers a clean and climate-friendly alternative to fossil-fuel gas and oil. Seattle has been a leader in reducing building emissions, including one of the nation's strongest energy codes, a program requiring owners of larger building to provide benchmarking data to the city and an aggressive tune-up program. There is still, however, more to be done to address buildings still reliant on fossil fuels and in need of efficiency upgrades, and to ensure future buildings have a positive impact on the city's emissions. To accomplish these goals, policies will first aim to spur actions through incentives and other measures, as well as leading efforts in City-owned buildings, with specific requirements when needed.

## Washington State tiered residential energy code

Adopt a tiered state residential energy code that can be adopted by cities.

Cities are currently only able to adopt a commercial energy code in Washington state, while the state controls the residential version. Seattle and other municipalities are interested in a tiered residential energy code, which would allow them to adopt an incrementally higher standard. State legislation would be required directing the State Building Code Council, which Seattle is a member of, to develop the tiered code. Higher tiers could also be used as the base State code in the following code cycle. Legislation to allow for tiered energy codes will be a priority for the City of Seattle in the 2019 legislative session.

## Establish new 2030 Challenge pilot for 20 upgraded, high performing projects by 2025

Create pilot program offering additional height and floor area incentives for significant upgrades in energy and water use, and transportation efficiency.

A new pilot will offer additional height and floor area incentives for up to 20 major renovations in urban centers outside the International District. Projects would receive the incentives in exchange for cutting energy and water use well below code, including no use of fossil fuels for heating. The plan additionally

<!-- image -->

calls for increasing the incentives for the existing Living Building Pilot, and adjusts penalties in line with the 2030 Challenge.

## Incentive-driven 2030 performance standards for commercial and multifamily buildings

Provide programs and incentives to spur improved energy efficiency and reduced carbon emissions, backed by a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030.

Energy use in existing commercial and large multifamily buildings represents approximately 55 percent of the city's building emissions, making a reduction in energy use and emissions in these buildings is critical to meeting our climate goals. Leading up to 2030, the city will work with building owners through incentives, technical assistance and other programs to help them become voluntary early adopters of the standards, and would then phase in performance requirements beginning in 2030. These programs would include, the existing Tune-Up Accelerator and Benchmarking market outreach, City Light's new Pay for Performance incentive, and the proposed 2030 Challenge High-Performance Existing Building Pilot, as well as additional opportunities. This action would build on existing work, including Benchmarking and the Building Tune-Up mandate.

## City Light Whole Building Pay for Performance (P4P) Programs

Scale Pay for Performance efforts and pilot an innovative utility program exploring Energy Efficiency as a Service in up to 30 buildings to unlock greater levels of energy efficiency depth at scale.

To address the 'hard to reach' energy savings, Seattle City Light is developing programs specifically aimed at enabling greater levels of energy efficiency depth in buildings. Whole building programs, such as Pay for Performance and Energy Efficiency as a Service (EEaS) are two approaches to increase energy savings in commercial buildings. Incentive payments are made over time based on measured energy savings and allow participants to bundle multiple projects and measures, across capital, operational & maintenance, and behavioral improvements.

Seattle City Light will pilot Energy Efficiency as a Service (EEaS), which is explicitly designed to help participants overcome the split incentive barrier in commercial buildings, where there is little motivation for a building owner or investor to finance deep energy retrofits whose benefits accrue to tenants. EEaS lets investors finance projects with a predictable return, owners generate a new revenue stream, and tenants occupy productive and energy efficient spaces. The pilot will leverage the lessons learned from a prototype at the Bullitt Center.

## Improve municipal building energy efficiency and reduce carbon emissions by 2025

Double existing budget allocation for reducing energy in municipal buildings from 2012-2015, with a goal of reducing energy use by 40 percent.

City-owned buildings comprise four percent of commercial building area of the city. The City will lead the way toward performance standards by aiming to reduce energy and emissions from our own building portfolio. Building on existing efforts to reduce energy use 20 percent by 2020, the City will double its budget allocation from 2021 to 2025, and set a new target to achieve an overall 40 percent energy and carbon emissions reduction in municipal buildings by 2025.

<!-- image -->

## Oil to heat pump conversion

Propose recommendations to mayor to convert 18,000 homes from heating oil to an electric heat pump

OSE will propose recommendations to the mayor aimed at accelerating the transition of 18,000 homes from heating with oil to an electric heat pump, and adequately serving those unable to finance the switch alone. Recommendations will include a financing plan to support low-income residents, as well as a combination of public and private incentives to spur action. Accomplishing this switch will reduce heating costs and minimize the threat of leaking tanks.

## Conclusion

The decision to withdraw the United States from the Paris Climate Agreement puts the health, wellbeing and very survival of people across the world at risk. It is imperative that cities across this nation step up and take meaningful climate action in the absence of federal leadership. By taking action, we are not only responding to the existential threat of climate change, but also making our local communities stronger, healthier, and more economically resilient.

Seattle is committed to meeting the goals of the Paris Climate Agreement. As we embrace our future as a large and rapidly growing city, we will make the choices necessary to care for our community, our economy and the planet today and for the future. Action at this scale requires a whole-city response, and a response that centers race and social justice; therefore, we will move these strategies forward in partnership with our residents, businesses, and civic organizations, with a focus on partnering with communities of color, Native peoples, immigrant and refugee communities, and low-income residents.

The near-term actions described in this strategy reflect the magnitude of the challenge before us. Doing our part under the Paris Climate Agreement requires that we transform both how we move around, how we heat and power our buildings, and where our energy comes from. Seattle City Light's clean and carbon neutral electricity is key to de-carbonizing Seattle's transportation and building systems, and we will increasingly leverage this invaluable resource to meet the needs of our growing city. These actions will not only result in significant GHG emissions reductions, but also position Seattle to continue to build this work as we become a global leader in defining what it means to be a climate-friendly city.

EXTRACTION CRITERIA:
This framework formalizes the workflow into a "Policy Extraction & Validation Protocol.'

## 1. Structural Discovery: The Outline Heuristic

NDCs are not standardized; they vary by country. To find policy-rich sections, you must look for specific keywords that signal the country's commitments.

## Standard Sections

- Mitigation: Actions aimed at reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (e.g., transitioning to renewables).
- Adaptation: Actions aimed at adjusting to the current and future effects of climate change (e.g., sea walls, drought-resistant crops).
- Means of Implementation (MoI): Where finance, technology transfer, and capacitybuilding are discussed.

## Non-Standard Indicators (Where to look if the above are missing)

If the outline is vague, look for these "Proxy Sections" in the Table of Contents:

- Sectoral Planning: Sections titled "Energy," "Transport," "Agriculture," or "Waste Management."
- Priority Areas: Often listed as "Key Pillars" or "Strategic Directions."
- Cross-Cutting Issues: Sections on gender, youth, or indigenous peoples often contain localized adaptation policies.
- Investment Portfolios: Lists of projects seeking international funding.

## 2. Extraction: The Policy Nomenclature

Policies are rarely labeled "Policy #1." Countries use diverse terminology to describe their commitments. A comprehensive extraction tool should scan for:

- Action-Oriented: Action Plan, Action Item, Measure, Initiative, Intervention, Program.
- Strategic: Roadmap, Strategy, Long-term Vision, Policy Framework, Master Plan.
- Regulatory: Legislative Act, Decree, Mandate, Building Code, Standard (e.g., MEPS Minimum Energy Performance Standards).
- Economic: Fiscal Instrument, Subsidy, Carbon Tax, Feed-in Tariff, Incentive Scheme.
- Project-Based: Pilot Project, Flagship Program, Infrastructure Investment.

all_policies.policy_statement: In 2011, the Mayor and Seattle City Council adopted a community-wide climate protection goal for Seattle to become carbon neutral by 2050 and directed creation of a plan to meet the goal (Resolution 31312).
all_policies.source_quote: In 2011, the Mayor and City Council adopted a bold climate protection goal for our community to become carbon neutral by 2050 and directed the creation of a plan to meet the goal (Resolution 31312). The resulting 2013 Climate Action Plan (CAP) provided a coordinated strategy aimed at reducing GHG emissions while also supporting other community goals, including building vibrant neighborhoods, fostering economic prosperity, and enhancing racial and social justice. The 2013 CAP included a slate of near-term actions - many of which were completed by 2015 - and more broadly defined longer-term strategies to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is an adopted formal goal and directive via a named City resolution with a quantified target and deadline (carbon neutral by 2050).

all_policies.policy_statement: In 2017, the City of Seattle amended the Seattle Electrical Code to require that new parking provide adequate electrical capacity for one electric vehicle charging station per parking space and that construction documents show equipment and conduit locations for future EV charging installation.
all_policies.source_quote:
## Electrical Code

In 2017, the Seattle Electrical Code was amended to ensure new parking is built to facilitate future electric vehicle charging infrastructure. The code requires adequate electrical capacity to serve one electric vehicle charging station per parking space and that construction documents show the location of equipment and conduit for future installation of electric vehicles charging stations.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is an enforceable code requirement specifying EV charging-readiness provisions for new parking.

all_policies.policy_statement: Seattle's Energy Benchmarking Program (SMC 22.920) requires owners of nonresidential and multi-family buildings 20,000 square feet or larger to track energy performance and annually report to the City; in 2016 the policy was updated to make reported data publicly available.
all_policies.source_quote: Adopted in 2010, Seattle's Energy Benchmarking Program (SMC 22.920) requires owners of nonresidential and multi-family buildings (20,000 square feet or larger) to track energy performance and annually report to the City. The policy was updated in 2016 to make reported data publicly available to further increase awareness of building energy use and support real estate market transformation. It is estimated that Seattle's benchmarked buildings represent about two-thirds of citywide commercial and industrial square footage. The Benchmarking and Transparency policy is foundational to reducing energy use and GHG emissions - raising the awareness of energy consumption among building owners and managers enables opportunities to reduce energy use and save money. The data also helps the City track overall building energy use and emissions while informing energy efficiency policy and program development. Program staff assist building owners with compliance, ensure data quality is high, and connect customers to rebates and technical assistance. Seattle has an industry leading compliance rate of 99 percent each of the past four years. Since 2014, buildings benchmarking three consecutive years have demonstrated a 2.7 percent decrease in energy use.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is an adopted municipal code requirement with clear scope (building types/size threshold) and a compliance mechanism (annual reporting); the quote also explicitly links to GHG emissions.

all_policies.policy_statement: The City of Seattle's Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930), adopted in 2016, requires commercial buildings 50,000 square feet or larger to identify low- or no-cost operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency, with compliance deadlines phased in by building size beginning in early 2019; a Qualified Tune-Ups Specialist must complete the assessment and report to the City.
all_policies.source_quote:
## Tune Ups

Adopted in 2016, the Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930) requires commercial buildings 50,000 square feet or larger to identifying low- or no-cost building operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency. Compliance deadlines will be phased in by building size, beginning in early 2019.  A Qualified Tune-Ups Specialist is required to complete the assessment, report to the City, and monitor implementation of operational and maintenance improvements. Examples of operational fixes include changes to thermostat set points, or adjusting lighting or irrigation schedules. Tune-ups also review HVAC, lighting, and water systems to identify needed maintenance, cleaning or repairs. These types of improvements typically reduce individual building energy use an estimated 10-15 percent. Across the entire commercial building sector, the tune-up mandate is expected to reduce energy use 5-8 percent and GHG emissions by 6-9 percent.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is an enforceable ordinance requirement with defined applicability and a stated compliance start date; the quote explicitly references GHG emissions impacts.

all_policies.policy_statement: The City of Seattle committed via Resolution 31652 to meet the Building Tune-Ups deadline for City buildings one year earlier than required for private owners.
all_policies.source_quote: To demonstrate leadership, build capacity in the industry, and help reduce compliance costs, the city has committed (Resolution 31652) to meeting the Building Tune-Ups deadline one year earlier than required for private owners.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is a formal City commitment referenced to a specific resolution with a clear timing requirement (one year earlier than private-owner deadlines).

all_policies.policy_statement: Seattle's Oil Heated Home Conversion program provides incentives for homeowners to replace oil heating systems with electric heat pumps and is converting 200 homes per year (launched July 2017).
all_policies.source_quote:
## Oil Heated Home Conversion

The Oil Heated Home Conversion program provides incentives for homeowners to replace oil heating systems with clean, efficient, electric heat pumps. By partnering with a heat pump distributor, who provides matching incentives, the program is converting 200 homes per year, while also influencing the home heating market so that electric heat pumps become a preferred heating system. Since its launch in July 2017, 135 homes have been converted with a GHG emissions savings of five MTCO2 per home.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is an implemented City incentive program with a quantified activity level (200 homes per year) and explicit GHG emissions savings.

all_policies.policy_statement: Seattle's 2015 Seattle Energy Code includes emissions criteria by requiring either non-fossil-fuel-based heating or more efficient windows for covered commercial buildings (including multifamily buildings four stories and above).
all_policies.source_quote:
## Energy Code

Seattle's commercial energy code (which includes multifamily buildings four stories and above) is a national leader. Approaches implemented first in Seattle are typically later adopted at the state level and in other leading North American cities.  An analysis of the 2012 Seattle Energy Code (SEC) found that commercial buildings meeting our code are, on average, 11 percent more efficient than those designed to the national standard, and the current code is approximately 20 percent more efficient. The 2015 SEC includes criteria that address emissions, by requiring either non-fossil fuel-based heating or more efficient windows. Seattle City Light provides an annual grant to Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections to help make possible the work to develop and implement Seattle's advanced code.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is a code requirement that explicitly addresses emissions through specified compliance pathways.

all_policies.policy_statement: In 2011, the City of Seattle updated its Sustainable Building Policy for City-owned buildings to require LEED Gold certification for new construction and major renovations and to expect projects to be 15 percent more energy efficient than the current code.
all_policies.source_quote: In 2011, the City updated its Sustainable Building Policy for City-owned buildings covering new construction and major renovations. In addition to the requirement to achieve LEED Gold certification, projects are expected to be 15 percent more energy efficient than the current code.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is a stated municipal policy requirement for City-owned building projects with a quantified efficiency expectation.

all_policies.policy_statement: In 2013, the City of Seattle adopted the Resource Conservation Management Plan (Resolution 31491) with a goal to achieve a 20 percent reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 from a 2008 baseline.
all_policies.source_quote: In 2013, the City adopted a Resource Conservation Management Plan (Resolution 31491), with the goal to achieve a 20 percent reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 (2008 baseline). The Office of Sustainability & Environment manages the dedicated funding and works with individual capital departments to prioritize, develop and implement energy efficiency projects. The City is on track to meet the reduction goal, with a 12 percent energy use reduction through the end of 2016.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is an adopted plan via resolution with a quantified target, deadline, and baseline; the quote also indicates dedicated funding is managed for implementation.

all_policies.policy_statement: Seattle's Green Fleet Action Plan guides the City's efforts to reduce municipal fleet GHG emissions by 50 percent by 2025 through fleet electrification, cleaner fuels where electrification is not feasible, improved efficiency of vehicle use, and procurement standards.
all_policies.source_quote: Seattle was one of the first cities in the country to buy conventional hybrids (early 2000s) and the battery electric Nissan Leaf (2011), install hybrid systems on ambulances, and use a 20 percent biodiesel blend from sustainable feedstocks in all heavy-duty vehicles. The Green Fleet Action Plan guides the City's efforts to meet the goal to reduce municipal fleet emissions by 50 percent by 2025 by increasingly electrifying the fleet, using cleaner fuels when electrification is not feasible, increasing efficiency in how vehicles are used, and setting standards for vehicle procurement. The City's fleet includes over 200 electric vehicles and over 300 hybrid vehicles. Between 2013 and 2016, GHG emissions from the municipal fleet decreased by 11.5 percent and total fuel use decreased by five percent.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is a quantified municipal fleet emissions-reduction target with a deadline and described mechanisms within a City plan.

all_policies.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will pass a new electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018 to ensure new construction or renovation of parking structures is built with electric vehicle infrastructure.
all_policies.source_quote:
## Electric vehicle readiness ordinance for new construction

Pass a new electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018, which will ensure new construction or renovation of parking structures is built with electric vehicle infrastructure.
all_policies.section_header: Electric vehicle readiness ordinance for new construction
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is a clear legislative commitment with a near-term deadline (2018) and a defined regulatory outcome (EV infrastructure in parking structures).

all_policies.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will release a map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018 to guide public and private investment in EV charging with a focus on equitable distribution.
all_policies.source_quote:
## Charging station network map & strategy

Release map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018.

While Seattle is one of the top US markets for electric vehicles, charging availability and convenience is a significant barrier to widespread adoption. An effective and just distribution of charging stations is critical to realizing the goal of 30 percent of light duty vehicles being electric by 2030, and to support electrification of professional fleets. With significant private sector interest in deploying charging stations across Seattle and the region, a charging station network map which demonstrates the City's strategy and outlines our technical and policy preferences (such as electric grid capacity, race and social justice outcomes, and electrification of shared fleets) will foster the most effective distribution of charging stations and help deploy private investment. The map will guide public and private investment in the network, based on a set of criteria, with a specific focus on equitable distribution of the city receiving significant public benefit when private entities lease space in the right of way. In developing the map, Seattle will work with regional partners with the goal of creating a network the recognizes how people move in and out of the city.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is an explicit City action with a stated 2018 deliverable; while it supports a broader EV goal, the commitment is the map release and use as an investment guide.

all_policies.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will create a new Green Fleet Action Plan by the end of 2018 to accelerate electrification of the municipal fleet and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles.
all_policies.source_quote:
## Green Fleet Action Plan update

Create a new Green Fleet Action Plan, by the end of 2018, to accelerate the electrification of the municipal fleet and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is a time-bound commitment to produce an updated City plan with explicit decarbonization mechanisms (electrification and fossil fuel phase-out) for municipal vehicles.

all_policies.policy_statement: Seattle's Mayor will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with City departments to define which major City projects to assess for GHG emissions, the assessment method, and how to account for broader costs of carbon, by October 2018.
all_policies.source_quote: City policies, plans and major investments have wide reaching and long-term climate impacts.  However, the City lacks a systematic way to assess the GHG emissions associated with major City actions, and to consider the cost of those emissions during the planning process. Creating such a system would help the City make better decisions in the short-term and be prepared for future financial impacts, such as carbon pricing. The Mayor will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with departments to define the types of projects to assess, the assessment method, and how to account for the broader costs of carbon, by October 2018.
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is a mayoral directive with a clear deadline (October 2018) to establish a systematic GHG assessment approach for City actions.

all_policies.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will prioritize legislation in the 2019 legislative session to allow for tiered residential energy codes in Washington State.
all_policies.source_quote: Cities are currently only able to adopt a commercial energy code in Washington state, while the state controls the residential version. Seattle and other municipalities are interested in a tiered residential energy code, which would allow them to adopt an incrementally higher standard. State legislation would be required directing the State Building Code Council, which Seattle is a member of, to develop the tiered code. Higher tiers could also be used as the base State code in the following code cycle. Legislation to allow for tiered energy codes will be a priority for the City of Seattle in the 2019 legislative session.
all_policies.section_header: Washington State tiered residential energy code
all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is an explicit City government legislative priority with a specified timeframe (2019 session) tied to energy code standards.

all_policies.source_quote: City-owned buildings comprise four percent of commercial building area of the city. The City will lead the way toward performance standards by aiming to reduce energy and emissions from our own building portfolio. Building on existing efforts to reduce energy use 20 percent by 2020, the City will double its budget allocation from 2021 to 2025, and set a new target to achieve an overall 40 percent energy and carbon emissions reduction in municipal buildings by 2025.

all_policies.extraction_rationale: This is a budget/resource commitment coupled with a quantified municipal target and deadline; the quote includes both the funding increase and the 2025 reduction target.

Adopted in 2016, the Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930) requires commercial buildings 50,000 square feet or larger to identifying low- or no-cost building operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency. Compliance deadlines will be phased in by building size, beginning in early 2019.  A Qualified Tune-Ups Specialist is required to complete the assessment, report to the City, and monitor implementation of operational and maintenance improvements. Examples of operational fixes include changes to thermostat set points, or adjusting lighting or irrigation schedules. Tune-ups also review HVAC, lighting, and water systems to identify needed maintenance, cleaning or repairs. These types of improvements typically reduce individual building energy use an estimated 10-15 percent. Across the entire commercial building sector, the tune-up mandate is expected to reduce energy use 5-8 percent and GHG emissions by 6-9 percent.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is an enforceable ordinance requirement with defined applicability and a stated compliance start date; the quote explicitly references GHG emissions impacts.

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle committed via Resolution 31652 to meet the Building Tune-Ups deadline for City buildings one year earlier than required for private owners.
dedup.source_quote: To demonstrate leadership, build capacity in the industry, and help reduce compliance costs, the city has committed (Resolution 31652) to meeting the Building Tune-Ups deadline one year earlier than required for private owners.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a formal City commitment referenced to a specific resolution with a clear timing requirement (one year earlier than private-owner deadlines).

dedup.policy_statement: Seattle's Oil Heated Home Conversion program provides incentives for homeowners to replace oil heating systems with electric heat pumps and is converting 200 homes per year (launched July 2017).
dedup.source_quote:
## Oil Heated Home Conversion

The Oil Heated Home Conversion program provides incentives for homeowners to replace oil heating systems with clean, efficient, electric heat pumps. By partnering with a heat pump distributor, who provides matching incentives, the program is converting 200 homes per year, while also influencing the home heating market so that electric heat pumps become a preferred heating system. Since its launch in July 2017, 135 homes have been converted with a GHG emissions savings of five MTCO2 per home.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is an implemented City incentive program with a quantified activity level (200 homes per year) and explicit GHG emissions savings.

dedup.policy_statement: Seattle's 2015 Seattle Energy Code includes emissions criteria by requiring either non-fossil-fuel-based heating or more efficient windows for covered commercial buildings (including multifamily buildings four stories and above).
dedup.source_quote:
## Energy Code

Seattle's commercial energy code (which includes multifamily buildings four stories and above) is a national leader. Approaches implemented first in Seattle are typically later adopted at the state level and in other leading North American cities.  An analysis of the 2012 Seattle Energy Code (SEC) found that commercial buildings meeting our code are, on average, 11 percent more efficient than those designed to the national standard, and the current code is approximately 20 percent more efficient. The 2015 SEC includes criteria that address emissions, by requiring either non-fossil fuel-based heating or more efficient windows. Seattle City Light provides an annual grant to Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections to help make possible the work to develop and implement Seattle's advanced code.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a code requirement that explicitly addresses emissions through specified compliance pathways.

dedup.policy_statement: Seattle's Green Fleet Action Plan guides the City's efforts to reduce municipal fleet GHG emissions by 50 percent by 2025 through fleet electrification, cleaner fuels where electrification is not feasible, improved efficiency of vehicle use, and procurement standards.
dedup.source_quote: Seattle was one of the first cities in the country to buy conventional hybrids (early 2000s) and the battery electric Nissan Leaf (2011), install hybrid systems on ambulances, and use a 20 percent biodiesel blend from sustainable feedstocks in all heavy-duty vehicles. The Green Fleet Action Plan guides the City's efforts to meet the goal to reduce municipal fleet emissions by 50 percent by 2025 by increasingly electrifying the fleet, using cleaner fuels when electrification is not feasible, increasing efficiency in how vehicles are used, and setting standards for vehicle procurement. The City's fleet includes over 200 electric vehicles and over 300 hybrid vehicles. Between 2013 and 2016, GHG emissions from the municipal fleet decreased by 11.5 percent and total fuel use decreased by five percent.

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will release a map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018 to guide public and private investment in EV charging with a focus on equitable distribution.
dedup.source_quote:
## Charging station network map & strategy

Release map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018.

While Seattle is one of the top US markets for electric vehicles, charging availability and convenience is a significant barrier to widespread adoption. An effective and just distribution of charging stations is critical to realizing the goal of 30 percent of light duty vehicles being electric by 2030, and to support electrification of professional fleets. With significant private sector interest in deploying charging stations across Seattle and the region, a charging station network map which demonstrates the City's strategy and outlines our technical and policy preferences (such as electric grid capacity, race and social justice outcomes, and electrification of shared fleets) will foster the most effective distribution of charging stations and help deploy private investment. The map will guide public and private investment in the network, based on a set of criteria, with a specific focus on equitable distribution of the city receiving significant public benefit when private entities lease space in the right of way. In developing the map, Seattle will work with regional partners with the goal of creating a network the recognizes how people move in and out of the city.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is an explicit City action with a stated 2018 deliverable; while it supports a broader EV goal, the commitment is the map release and use as an investment guide.

The Mayor will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with departments to define the types of projects to assess, the assessment method, and how to account for the broader costs of carbon, by October 2018.

prompt.content:
## Extraction
You are a climate policy analyst. Your task is to extract climate policies from a long policy document with high precision (avoid spurious “policy-like” facts).

For each extracted policy, produce a JSON object with these fields:

EXTRACTION FIELDS
- "policy_statement": concise, self-contained commitment that preserves: (a) actor, (b) sector/scope (e.g., municipal vs citywide), (c) action/mechanism, and (d) any targets, baseline, and deadlines. Write it so it can stand alone outside the document.
- "source_quote": verbatim quote (typically 1–3 sentences) that directly contains the commitment. Do not stitch together non-adjacent text. If a policy has multiple key parts in the same paragraph (e.g., funding + target), include the sentence(s) covering all key parts.
- "section_header": the nearest section/subsection heading that governs the quoted text (copy from document).
- "extraction_rationale": 1–2 sentences explaining why it is a policy and noting any missing specifics (e.g., no timeline), or why you split/merged items.

WHAT COUNTS AS A POLICY (TIGHTENED)
Extract ONLY items that are clearly a government (or named agency/department) commitment, requirement, adoption, or funded action. A policy must include at least one strong anchor:

STRONG POLICY ANCHORS (extract)
1) Adopted/approved instrument: ordinance, resolution, code/standard adoption, plan/program launch, executive order, contract, formal strategy with commitments.
2) Enforceable requirement: “require,” “must,” “prohibit,” “mandate,” “standard,” “code requires…”
3) Budget/resource commitment: dollars, budget changes (e.g., “double funding”), staffing, procurement commitment.
4) Quantified target WITH scope: numeric target + timeframe (and baseline if stated) tied to a responsible actor (City, department, utility) and a defined scope (e.g., “City-owned buildings,” “municipal fleet”).

WEAK/AMBIGUOUS ITEMS (do NOT extract unless upgraded by a strong anchor)
- Descriptive status or progress: “on track,” “has reduced,” “currently,” “as of…”
- General goals/aspirations without mechanism or responsible actor: “aim to,” “support,” “encourage,” “work toward,” “seek to,” “promote”
- Explanations of what a code/program is, unless the text states an actual requirement or adoption applicable in the jurisdiction.
- Forecasts, potentials, benefits, rationale, stakeholder/process steps, studies, pilots described only as concepts (unless a launch/implementation commitment is stated).

SCOPE & SPECIFICITY RULES (to improve match quality)
- Preserve scope exactly: distinguish “municipal/City-owned operations” vs “citywide/community-wide.” If the text is about City-owned buildings, do NOT rewrite as “buildings sector” or “citywide buildings.”
- Prefer the most specific commitment over a derived/summary metric. If the document provides an operational target and/or funding mechanism (e.g., “double budget 2021–2025” + “reduce municipal building energy 40% by 2025”), extract that, not a broader “on track to meet city goal…”.
- Include all key components that are stated together: if a policy sentence lists multiple measures or a two-part commitment (e.g., two pilots; funding + target; target + baseline), capture them in ONE policy_statement when they are clearly part of the same commitment. Only split if they are independent actions not linked by the text.

DEDUPLICATION / GRANULARITY
- Deduplicate true duplicates (same actor + action + target/timeline), keeping the most detailed version.
- Do not “invent” new policies by generalizing a described feature into a commitment. If unsure whether it is descriptive vs mandatory, do NOT extract.

STRATEGY
1) Process section by section using headers as anchors.
2) In each section, extract only statements meeting the strong-anchor test; prioritize specificity (actor/scope/mechanism/target).
3) When a section mixes “policy context” with “requirements/commitments,” extract only the requirements/commitments and quote them.
4) Collect extracted policies into a single Python list of dicts, deduplicate, store as `all_policies`, and call FINAL_VAR(all_policies).

OUTPUT FORMAT
Your final answer MUST be a valid JSON list of policy objects as described above.

## Hierarchy
EXTRACTION FIELDS (hierarchy-related only):
- "role": "individual" | "sub" | "parent"
    • "individual": standalone policy, no parent-child relationship
    • "sub": specific action listed under a named parent initiative (e.g. lettered or numbered list items A., B., C.)
    • "parent": umbrella initiative/program that has sub-actions listed beneath it
- "parent_statement": the name or summary of the parent initiative for "sub" role only. Use null for "individual" and "parent".

HIERARCHY RULES:
- When you see a named initiative followed by lettered or numbered sub-items, extract the initiative header as "parent" AND each sub-item as "sub" with parent_statement pointing to that initiative name.
- If a policy stands alone with no sub-items beneath it, it is "individual".
- When in doubt between "parent" and "individual", prefer "individual" unless there are clear sub-items.

## Classification
CLASSIFICATION FIELDS — assign alongside extraction (be conservative to reduce spurious “climate policy” labeling):

- "primary_category": one of "Mitigation" | "Adaptation" | "Resource Efficiency" | "Nature-Based Solutions"
  Choose the category that matches the policy’s *explicit* main mechanism in the quoted text.
  • Mitigation: explicit GHG/carbon reductions, decarbonization, renewable energy, electrification, carbon neutrality targets, sequestration (when framed as carbon storage).
  • Adaptation: explicit resilience to climate hazards/impacts (heat, wildfire smoke, flooding/sea level rise, drought, stormwater extremes), preparedness, risk reduction.
  • Resource Efficiency: explicit efficiency/conservation (energy efficiency, reduced energy use, water conservation, waste/material efficiency) *without* an explicit carbon/GHG framing as the main driver.
  • Nature-Based Solutions: explicit ecosystem/green infrastructure actions (tree canopy, wetlands, habitat restoration, green stormwater infrastructure) as the main mechanism.
  If the text is only a generic commitment (“support climate goals”, “identify actions”, “create a plan”) and does not specify the mechanism, still choose the most directly stated intent (often Mitigation if it names carbon neutrality/Paris/1.5°C), but do not “upgrade” vague non-climate plans into climate categories.

- "financial_instrument": "yes" | "no"
  Mark "yes" only when the policy itself *creates/changes/commits* money flows or a pricing tool in the quoted text, e.g.:
  • taxes/fees/levies, carbon price tools, rebates, grants, subsidies, tax credits, loans/bonds
  • creation of a fund/trust, explicit budget appropriation, explicit “allocate $X”, “increase budget by X%”, “double the budget”, “invest $X”
  Otherwise "no" (including: adopting a plan, directing staff, setting targets, installing infrastructure, implementing regulations—unless the funding mechanism is explicitly part of the policy statement).

- "climate_relevance": "direct" | "indirect" | "peripheral"
  Use the most conservative label supported by the policy_statement/source_quote.
  • "direct": the text explicitly states climate change, GHG/carbon/emissions, decarbonization, Paris/1.5°C, carbon neutrality, or named climate hazards/impacts (heat, flooding/sea level rise, wildfire smoke, drought) as the objective.
  • "indirect": the objective is primarily non-climate (cost savings, general energy efficiency, air quality, transportation performance, asset management) but the text explicitly frames it as contributing to climate goals *or* clearly targets major emitting sectors (building energy efficiency, fleet fuel switching, EV charging) without explicit climate language.
  • "peripheral": the climate link is not stated and would be speculative (general sustainability language, generic planning/management, routine capital maintenance).
  Important: do not label something "direct" solely because it is in a climate plan/background section; rely on explicit objective language in the quote.

- "secondary_category": one of "Mitigation" | "Adaptation" | "Resource Efficiency" | "Nature-Based Solutions" | null
  Assign a secondary category only when the policy text explicitly states a second distinct climate mechanism (not implied co-benefits, not elsewhere in the document). If unclear, use null.
  Decision table (triggers must be explicit in THIS policy’s quoted text):
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Primary              │ Type  │ Trigger (must be explicit in text)      │ Secondary        │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Mitigation           │ M-1   │ Named efficiency action/energy-use cut    │ Resource Eff.    │
  │ Mitigation           │ M-2   │ Named climate hazard + resilience measure │ Adaptation       │
  │ Mitigation           │ M-3   │ Biological sequestration stated           │ Nature-Based Sol.│
  │ Resource Efficiency  │ RE-1  │ Explicit GHG/carbon/emissions target      │ Mitigation       │
  │ Resource Efficiency  │ RE-2  │ Named climate hazard motivates measure    │ Adaptation       │
  │ Resource Efficiency  │ RE-3  │ Ecosystem/green infra is the mechanism    │ Nature-Based Sol.│
  │ Nature-Based Sol.    │ NBS-1 │ Named climate hazard addressed by NBS     │ Adaptation       │
  │ Nature-Based Sol.    │ NBS-2 │ Carbon sequestration explicitly stated    │ Mitigation       │
  │ Nature-Based Sol.    │ NBS-3 │ Explicit resource savings/efficiency goal │ Resource Eff.    │
  │ Adaptation           │ A-1   │ Ecosystem/green infra named as mechanism  │ Nature-Based Sol.│
  │ Adaptation           │ A-2   │ Explicit efficiency measure named         │ Resource Eff.    │
  │ Adaptation           │ A-3   │ Explicit GHG/carbon reduction component   │ Mitigation       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Common errors to avoid:
  • Do NOT add Mitigation secondary to Resource Efficiency just because efficiency reduces emissions (requires explicit GHG/carbon/emissions language).
  • Do NOT add Adaptation secondary to NBS unless a named hazard/impact is stated in the same policy.
  • Do NOT assign a secondary category from context like “Paris Agreement” unless the policy text also states a second mechanism (e.g., efficiency + emissions).
  • Do NOT treat “disaster risk mitigation” as GHG Mitigation unless emissions/carbon is explicitly referenced.
